name: Universal mixture / infinite divisibility of matter
plain_explanation: Anaxagoras thought every piece of matter, no matter how small, contains a bit of every kind of stuff there is; something just looks like 'fire' or 'water' because that ingredient predominates in it.
precise_definition: The doctrine that matter is infinitely divisible and that every portion of matter, however small, contains some portion of every element; a thing is called by the name of whichever element preponderates within it (e.g., something is called 'fire' because fire predominates, though it also contains portions of everything else, including, Anaxagoras held, some blackness even in snow).
why_it_mattered: It is Anaxagoras's distinctive solution to the problem, shared with other post-Parmenidean philosophers, of accounting for apparent change and plurality without admitting real coming-into-being or passing-away of substance.
historical_origin: A response to Parmenides's arguments against absolute generation and destruction, worked out independently of Empedocles's four-element theory.
examples: Everything contains some fire, but is only called 'fire' if fire predominates
Snow is (in part) black, according to Anaxagoras
competing_positions: Empedocles's theory of four unchanging elements (earth, air, fire, water) mixed in different proportions
